title: Ukraine's Drone War on Russian Oil, Mapped
description:
Ukraine says its long-range drones have knocked out more than half of Russia's oil refining capacity. Russia says it shoots most of them down, and keeps striking Ukraine's power grid in return. Here is the map of the refinery war: how far the drones fly, which plants have been hit, what it has done to Russian fuel, and why Washington asked Kyiv to pause.

Facts as reported up to 1 November 2026, from Ukraine's Defence Ministry, the Russian Defence Ministry, the IEA, the Associated Press, the Kyiv Independent and others (sources below). Claims from either side are attributed and could not all be independently verified.

Maps: country borders as shown by the Survey of India (Natural Earth, India view). Satellite imagery: NASA Blue Marble; contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2025-2026.
core_message: Cheap long-range drones let Ukraine hit refineries over a thousand kilometres away, and the fuel war now shapes the whole conflict.
comment_question: Should refineries be off limits in a ceasefire, or are they fair targets in war?

scenes.narration: On the morning of the twenty-ninth of October, Russia's defence ministry said it had intercepted one thousand two hundred and fourteen Ukrainian drones over its territory.
scenes.heading: 1,214 drones, says Moscow

scenes.narration: Moscow's mayor said six hundred and thirteen of them flew towards the capital region. Three of the city's four airports had to restrict flights overnight.
Russia says it shot most of them down. But a few days later, three more Russian oil refineries were burning.
This is the other front of the war in Ukraine: a fight over fuel, fought with drones that fly a thousand kilometres or more.
Why refineries? Oil and fuel pay for a large part of Russia's state budget, and its army runs on diesel.
Crude oil is hard to destroy. It sits in pipelines and tanks, and it can be pumped out again. A refinery is different.
scenes.text: Crude is hard to hit. Refineries aren't.

scenes.narration: At its heart is a distillation unit, a tall column where crude is boiled and split into petrol, diesel and jet fuel. Hit that column, and the whole plant can stop.
scenes.text: One column runs the whole plant

scenes.narration: Russia has about thirty-two large refineries. The International Energy Agency says some have been hit as many as fifteen times since the war began.
Here is how far the drones fly. From Ukrainian-held territory to the refinery in Moscow is more than five hundred kilometres.
scenes.heading: To Moscow

scenes.narration: Further north, Yaroslavl and the Kirishi refinery near Saint Petersburg have both been hit.
scenes.heading: North: Yaroslavl and Kirishi

scenes.narration: East along the Volga are Saratov, Syzran and Novokuibyshevsk near Samara.
scenes.heading: The Volga refineries

scenes.narration: And past the Volga, Ufa in Bashkortostan and Perm, near the Ural Mountains, more than one thousand five hundred kilometres from Ukraine.
scenes.heading: Out to the Urals

scenes.narration: According to the Kyiv Independent, Ukraine's drones and missiles now regularly hit targets more than fifteen hundred kilometres away. The longest strike so far, on a gas facility in September, was about three thousand two hundred kilometres.
The best known of these drones is the FP-1, built by the Ukrainian company Fire Point. Ukraine's defence ministry says it tripled production of long-range strike drones this year.
The idea is simple: launch so many cheap drones that air defences can't stop them all, and only a few need to get through.
scenes.text: Only a few need to get through

scenes.narration: Overnight on the thirtieth of October, drones hit the Novokuibyshevsk refinery in the Samara region, and it caught fire.
scenes.heading: 30 October: Novokuibyshevsk

scenes.narration: On the thirty-first, the Bashneft Novoil refinery in Ufa.
scenes.heading: 31 October: Ufa

scenes.narration: And overnight on the first of November, LUKOIL's big refinery at Kstovo, near Nizhny Novgorod, which also caught fire.
scenes.heading: 1 November: Kstovo

scenes.narration: Together, those three plants can process about thirty-three million tonnes of crude a year, roughly a tenth of Russia's refining capacity. How much damage was done has not been independently confirmed.
scenes.heading: Capacity of the three plants

scenes.narration: Russia does not publish figures on damage to its refineries. In September, President Putin signed a decree restricting access to data on refineries and energy exports.
On the fourth of October, Ukraine's defence ministry claimed that more than half of Russia's refining capacity had been disabled. That claim could not be independently verified.
scenes.heading: Ukraine's claim: refining capacity disabled

scenes.narration: But there are signs from outside Ukraine too. The IEA says Russian diesel output fell by about thirty percent, and that drivers waited up to forty hours to fill up.
The Kremlin banned diesel exports, which pushed up diesel prices around the world.
Refiners have delayed maintenance, restarted old mothballed units and lowered fuel quality standards to keep fuel flowing.
On the first of October, Vladimir Putin said the strikes had cost Russia roughly one percent of its GDP. Asked whether Ukraine had achieved its goal, he said: partially.
scenes.author: Vladimir Putin, 1 October 2026, on whether the strikes achieved their goal

scenes.narration: Repeated damage and rushed repairs can wear units down for years, the IEA warns.
Russia has its own long-range campaign. It sends waves of Shahed-type drones and missiles at Ukraine's power stations, substations and ports.
scenes.heading: Russia's strikes on Ukraine

scenes.narration: Overnight into the fifth of October, Ukraine's air force said Russia launched two hundred and five drones, and that one hundred and seventy-two were shot down or jammed.
That same day, a Russian guided bomb in Kharkiv killed at least three people, and a drone sank a commercial ship in the Black Sea.
scenes.text: A city and a ship hit

scenes.narration: The refinery strikes worry Washington too. On the thirteenth of September, President Trump urged Ukraine to stop hitting refineries.
In October, Kyiv paused refinery strikes for three days at Washington's request. On the fifteenth, President Zelenskyy said the restrictions had been lifted.
Ukrainian analysts say there was a second, informal pause of about two weeks. It ended with the three strikes at the end of October.
Fuel has become a bargaining chip. Whatever peace talks come next, the refineries along the Volga will be on the table.
scenes.heading: The refinery map

scenes.narration: So what to watch? Whether Russia's air defences can thin out the swarms. Whether repairs keep up with the damage. And whether a ceasefire puts energy off limits for both sides.
scenes.heading: What to watch
items: Can air defences thin the swarms?
Will a ceasefire protect energy on both sides?

scenes.narration: A thousand kilometres used to be safe distance from a front line. In this war, it isn't any more.
scenes.heading: No longer out of reach

scenes.narration: Should refineries be off limits in a ceasefire, or are they fair targets in war? Tell us in the comments.
